summary: For ages 7–9: the ocean has three zones defined by depth and light — the sunlight zone near the surface (most life), the twilight zone where light fades, and the midnight zone of total darkness. Two linked ideas: (1) light decreases with depth until it is gone; (2) because plants (phytoplankton/algae) need light to make food, most life clusters in the thin sunlit surface layer. The vertical scale matters: the sunlit layer is a thin skin over a vast dark deep. Activities build from naming the zones top-to-bottom, to stating that light fades to nothing, to explaining why most life gathers where the light is.
misconceptions: 'The ocean is equally full of life all the way down' — not grasping life concentrates near the sunlit surface.
'It's dark deep down because it's far from the sky/space' — rather than because water absorbs and scatters light with depth.
'The zones are equal in size' — missing that the sunlit layer is a thin skin over a vast dark deep.
'Plants grow on the deep ocean floor like on land' — not connecting no-light with no-photosynthesis.
Treating the zone boundaries as sharp walls rather than gradual fades in light.

activities.title: Scroll down a to-scale ocean cross-section
steps: Explore a tall, roughly-to-scale vertical cross-section of the ocean, moving from the bright surface down into total darkness.
Identify each of the three zones in order from top to bottom: sunlight, twilight, midnight.
Watch or track a light indicator (e.g. a side gauge or a fading colour bar) that drops toward zero as depth increases.
Note the characteristic residents of each band — e.g. dolphins and shoals of fish near the surface, a lanternfish in the twilight gloom, an anglerfish with its lure in the dark midnight zone.
Compare the thickness of the sunlit layer with the vast dark depths below it.
Follow a 'why is the top so full of life?' explanation that traces sunlight → phytoplankton → food → most life.
activities.insight: Light fades with depth through three named zones, and the bright, crowded sunlight zone is only a thin skin at the very top, because plants need light to make food so life crowds where the light is.

activities.title: Pilot a submersible down through the zones
steps: Control a descending submersible using a depth slider, watching ambient light dim in real time as depth increases.
Read a light-meter that moves toward zero as the sub goes deeper.
Switch on a headlamp as the twilight zone becomes too dim to see well, and keep it on in the midnight zone, where no sunlight is left.
Notice that the life encountered thins out with increasing depth.
activities.insight: Daylight drains to black as you descend, and you must bring your own light to see in the deep — making the light-fade something you act on rather than just read.

activities.title: Connect to how light behaves in water
steps: Recall prior learning that light travels and that we see things because light enters our eyes.
Investigate or observe light shining through more and more water, using slightly tinted or milky water as a model of many metres of seawater, and describe how it dims.
Explain, in their own words, why it gets dark deep down — because water absorbs and scatters light with depth, not because the deep is 'far from the sky or space'.
State that light fades gradually with depth rather than switching off suddenly.
activities.insight: The deep ocean is dark because water absorbs and scatters sunlight as it travels down, so 'why does it get dark?' is grounded in how light behaves, not just asserted.

activities.title: Explain and check the light–life connection
steps: Put the three zones in order by depth, top to bottom.
Answer: what happens to light as you go deeper? (It fades until it is gone.)
Answer and explain: which zone has the most life, and why? (The sunlight zone — plants need light to make food.)
Respond to a claim such as 'The deep bottom must be where MOST sea life lives — there's the most room down there' by saying whether it is right and explaining why.
Consider a counterexample: a deep-sea anglerfish does live in the midnight zone with no sunlight — discuss how life can still exist deep, but differently, even though most life is near the surface.
Answer: could a seaweed grow on the deep dark seabed? Why or why not?
activities.insight: Most ocean life lives near the surface because plants need light to make food and form the base of the food chain; light fades through twilight to a dark midnight zone — yet some life still survives deeper by other means.

checkQuestion: A child says: 'The deep bottom of the ocean must be where MOST sea life lives — there's the most room down there.' Is that right? Tell me which zone has the most life and why, and what happens to sunlight as you go deeper and deeper.
checkAnswer: It's not right — most ocean life lives near the TOP, in the sunlight zone, not the deep bottom. As you go deeper, sunlight fades: through the twilight zone where light is dim, down to the midnight zone which is totally dark. Tiny plants (phytoplankton) need light to grow and make food, and they are the base of the food chain, so most animals gather near the surface where there is light and food.
